original:
Tea cools faster in a wide mug mainly because of surface area. Most of the heat leaves through the top of the drink, and a wide mug exposes far more of it to the air.

Evaporation is the biggest factor. The fastest-moving water molecules at the surface escape as vapor, and each one carries away a lot of energy. A larger surface lets more molecules escape every second, so the tea loses heat quickly. This is why blowing across a cup cools it: you sweep away the humid air above the surface and speed up evaporation.

Convection adds to this. Air touching the hot surface warms and rises, and cooler air moves in to replace it. A wide surface drives more of this circulation.

Radiation also contributes. Hot liquid emits infrared energy, and a bigger exposed area emits more of it.

The mug's sides lose heat too, but they matter less. A tall, narrow mug holds the same volume with less surface on top, so it cools more slowly.

To keep tea hot, use a narrow mug, add a lid, or both. A lid stops evaporation and traps the warm air above the tea.

Evaporation does the most damage. The fastest-moving water molecules at the surface escape as vapor, and each one takes a lot of energy with it. A larger surface lets more of them escape every second, so the tea loses heat quickly. That's why blowing across a cup cools it: you sweep off the humid air sitting above the surface, and evaporation speeds up.

Convection adds to this. Air touching the hot surface warms and rises, and cooler air moves in to take its place. The wider the surface, the more of that circulation it drives.

Radiation plays a part too. Hot liquid gives off infrared energy, and a bigger exposed area gives off more of it.

The mug's sides lose heat as well, but they don't matter as much. A tall, narrow mug holds the same volume with less surface on top. It cools more slowly.

If you want to keep tea hot, use a narrow mug, add a lid, or do both. A lid blocks evaporation and traps the warm air above the tea.
